clue.text: Asian shot, in the wars endlessly

indicators.note: the shot is placed inside the trimmed name of the wars
the last letter of the wars' name is dropped, leaving it without an end

parts.note: the Punic Wars were fought between Rome and Carthage
a jab is a quick shot or punch, or an injection

explanation.surface: An Asian person has been shot while caught up in endless fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' looks like a gunshot victim, but it is a jab, as from a needle or a boxer's fist.
explanation.definitionFit: A Punjabi is a person from the Punjab region of India and Pakistan, so an Asian.

parts.note: read as 'in the way of Thomas More's ideal', his imagined perfect island state, which also describes something idealistic

explanation.surface: Something is made more perfect in this way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More' looks like a comparative, but it is Sir Thomas More, who wrote of an ideal island commonwealth.
explanation.definitionFit: Visionary and idealistic, like the perfect society Thomas More imagined in his famous book.

clue.text: Hear legend captured by obscure character

indicators.note: one piece is held inside the other, as a captive is held

parts.note: Jude the Obscure is the title character of Thomas Hardy's novel
read as 'leg end', the final letter of the word leg

explanation.surface: Listening to a myth that a mysterious figure has seized upon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'legend' splits as leg-end, giving G, and 'captured by' puts it inside JUDE, Hardy's 'obscure' hero.
explanation.definitionFit: To hear a case in court is to try it and decide, as one presiding does.

clue.text: Islander's written about the sign of an illiterate 22

indicators.note: the islander's word is written around the sign

parts.note: a Briton is an inhabitant of the British Isles; the 's stands for 'is'
someone who cannot write signs with a cross

explanation.surface: A man from an island has written around the mark made by someone who cannot sign his name.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is the first part of a linked answer, PRISON. 'written about' puts X inside BRITON. BRIXTON is a prison in south London.
explanation.definitionFit: Brixton is a well-known men's jail in south London, so an example of the cross-referenced word.

clue.text: Pork faked in bed for swingers

parts.note: ham is pork from the leg
mock means imitation or faked

explanation.surface: Imitation pork found lying in bed for a party set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swingers' suggests a racy party, but here it means people who swing in their bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A hammock is a hanging bed of canvas or net that swings between two supports.

clue.text: Dictator in Los Angeles brought up to be a brute

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising the pieces means reading them from the bottom up
the dictator's name sits inside the city's abbreviation

parts.note: Idi Amin was the dictator of Uganda

explanation.surface: A tyrant raised in California grows up to be a savage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' works because this is a down clue: the letters read from the bottom upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A brute is a beast or savage creature, as is an animal in the insulting sense.

indicators.note: the order with its time goes inside the state's name

parts.note: Maine is a US state

indicators.note: the time letter goes inside the order's abbreviation

parts.note: the DSO is the Distinguished Service Order, a British military honour

explanation.surface: Serving time in an orderly way in a state prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is PRISON, the first word of the linked answer. MAIDSTONE is a prison in Kent; 'order' is a British decoration, not a sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Maidstone, the county town of Kent, has a long-established jail, so an example of the cross-referenced word.

clue.text: Feature of motorway about to enter European city

indicators.note: the motorway feature goes around the other piece

parts.note: traffic cones are a familiar sight on motorways
to log something is to enter it in a record

explanation.surface: Roadworks ahead as a driver nears a continental city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to enter' looks like part of the picture of arriving at a city, but it means to record something.
explanation.definitionFit: Cologne is a large German city on the Rhine, hence one in Europe.

parts.note: Jerry is old slang for a German
a springer is a spaniel breed

explanation.surface: A display of dogs from Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dog show' suggests Crufts, but the show is the American talk programme named after its host.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jerry Springer Show was a notorious American TV talk show; the question mark marks the definition by example.

definitions.meaning: Gerald ... was the 38th President of the United States
An open jail in West Sussex

explanation.surface: An American leader is locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is PRISON; Ford open prison is in West Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: Gerald was the US leader after Nixon, and Ford is a Sussex jail.

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the abbreviation for good is to be removed from the word for insignificant

parts.note: negligible means too small to matter

explanation.surface: Someone unimportant and no good is not qualified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no good' looks like a verdict, but 'no' removes G from NEGLIGIBLE to leave NELIGIBLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ineligible means not qualified or entitled to be chosen, such as for a post.

parts.note: W stands for west, a compass bearing
id est is the Latin for 'that is', usually shortened to i.e.

explanation.surface: Being as broad as possible in one's direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that is' gives the full Latin phrase id est, not just its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Widest is the superlative of wide, meaning broadest or most extensive.

clue.text: Could be no stopping adoring fans ultimately going mad

indicators.note: the letters lose their senses and are rearranged
the final letter of fans is taken

explanation.surface: Fans in a frenzy cannot be halted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes S from fans, and 'going mad' scrambles it with ADORING.
explanation.definitionFit: A notice reading 'no stopping' is one example of a traffic sign, hence 'could be'.

clue.text: Unsuitable quality rejected in Spain, unfortunately

indicators.note: the rejected piece sits inside the scrambled country
the country's letters suffer a mishap and are rearranged

parts.note: rejected read as sent back: the word sent written backwards

explanation.surface: Being turned down in Spain was unlucky and inappropriate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' turns SPAIN into INAPS; 'rejected' is read as 'sent back', giving its letters in reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Inaptness is the state of being unsuitable or inappropriate, so it is an unsuitable quality.

parts.note: to park is to stop a vehicle

indicators.note: the word for suffering goes around the skin's first letter

parts.note: hurt means pain or suffering
read as skin's head, the first letter of the word skin

explanation.surface: Stop beating up the shaven-headed man in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is PRISON. 'skinhead' looks like a shaven youth but is read as the head of skin. PARKHURST is a prison on the Isle of Wight.
explanation.definitionFit: Parkhurst is a famous high-security jail on the Isle of Wight, so an example of the cross-referenced word.

definitions.meaning: George Foreman is a heavyweight boxing champion; the 's stands for 'is'
a type of German breed of dog with a square muzzle

explanation.surface: Does the works manager own a dog?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreman' looks like a works supervisor, but he is George Foreman, the boxing champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: George Foreman fought in the ring, and the breed is a German dog.

definitions.meaning: twenty, written in Roman numerals, is a set of twenty
a mark or grade given to judge something

explanation.surface: A film certificate marked twice with X.
explanation.walkthrough: XX looks like a film classification, but it is the Roman numeral for twenty.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is a group of twenty, and a score is also a mark given as a rating.

clue.text: Beginning to crease, crease and crease

indicators.note: the first letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: to rumple is to crease or wrinkle

explanation.surface: A fold starts to form, then another, then another.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word appears three times with three jobs: a letter, a synonym, and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To crumple is to crush into creases or wrinkles, so it means to crease.

clue.text: Church involved in issue on location in New Jersey

indicators.note: the church abbreviation is wrapped up inside the word for issue

parts.note: to print a book is to issue it
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church is caught up in a dispute about a place in the eastern United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' looks like a dispute, but it means PRINT, as in publishing.
explanation.definitionFit: Princeton is a university town in New Jersey, so a place there.

indicators.note: the final letter of the word for singing is cut off

parts.note: to trill is to sing with a warbling sound

explanation.surface: The opening numbers are left incomplete by the singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening numbers' looks like a concert's first songs, but 'Opening' is the definition, a hole in the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostril is one of the two openings of the nose.

parts.note: read not as a crime with help from within but as employment inside a jail, guarding those locked up

explanation.surface: A crime committed with help from someone on the staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside job' usually means a crime by an insider; here 'inside' is slang for in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: A jail warder's work is literally done inside, where convicts are, and 'inside' is slang for imprisoned.

indicators.note: the letters are formed again into a new order

explanation.surface: A disciple of a Protestant reformer later changes the barbarian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reforming' echoes the Reformation in the surface but signals the rearrangement of HUN LATER.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Martin Luther, the leader of the Protestant Reformation, is called after him.

indicators.note: licked as in beaten, so the letters are knocked about

parts.note: ff is fortissimo, the musical mark for very loud and strong

explanation.surface: Someone licks the paper of a very potent smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'licked' is what you do to a rolling paper, but here it means beaten, rearranging LIPS to SPLI.
explanation.definitionFit: A spliff is a hand-rolled cannabis cigarette, slang often heard in Britain.

clue.text: 22 where art critic almost hauled up

indicators.note: in a down clue, hauling up means reading from the bottom upwards
the critic's surname loses its final letter

parts.note: Brian Sewell was a well-known British art critic

explanation.surface: An art critic was nearly dragged off to jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is PRISON. 'almost' trims SEWELL to SEWEL and 'hauled up' turns it over in this down clue. LEWES is a prison in East Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewes, the county town of East Sussex, has a jail, so an example of the cross-referenced word.

clue.text: Spike pierced by worst sort of spikes, perhaps

indicators.note: the spike has the other piece driven into it

parts.note: a spear is a long pointed weapon, a spike

indicators.note: the letters are sorted into a different order

explanation.surface: A weapon is stabbed by some unpleasant kind of spike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spikes' in the definition are running shoes with studs, which is why 'perhaps' follows; the surface makes them weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Spikes are running shoes with studs, an example of athletic clothing, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Highland town where women's 22 going topless

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for women

indicators.note: the first letter, the top in an across answer, is removed

parts.note: nick is British slang for a jail, the cross-referenced word

explanation.surface: Women's jail where the inmates go bare-chested in the Scottish north.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is PRISON, and NICK is British slang for it; 'going topless' drops its N. WICK is a town in Caithness, in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Wick is a town on the far north-east coast of Scotland, in the Highland region.

clue.text: My job is turning to jelly

definitions.meaning: the compiler's own work is making crosswords
a jelly firming up as it cools

explanation.surface: The speaker confesses that work is making them go weak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is the crossword compiler speaking: the setter's job is composing the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter's work is composing puzzles, and a liquid becoming firm, like jelly, is also this.

indicators.note: the letters are written again in a new order

explanation.surface: A setter is told to end by redrafting the clues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewrite' signals that CLUES OR is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A closure is an end or conclusion, as of a meeting or a business.
